ChatGPT said:

For NephroReach, I would keep the Provider portal focused on viewing patient-generated information, communicating, and optionally entering selected care information—not turning NephroReach into a full EHR. That keeps the build manageable while still making the B2B product valuable.

Here is a response you can send directly to the developers:

NephroReach – Provider & Caregiver System Requirements

1. What patient information can the Provider view?

Providers should only be able to view patients who are assigned/enrolled under their specific facility or organization. Providers from one organization must NEVER be able to access another organization’s patients.

For an assigned patient, the Provider should be able to view:

Patient Profile

  • Patient name

  • Date of birth

  • Preferred contact information

  • Emergency contact

  • Dialysis modality: In-center HD, Home Hemodialysis, Peritoneal Dialysis, CKD/not yet on dialysis

  • Dialysis facility

  • Nephrologist/provider

  • Treatment schedule

  • Estimated dry weight

  • Vascular access type

  • Patient enrollment/status

Patient Logs

Providers should be able to view patient-entered information including:

  • Blood pressure logs

  • Weight/fluid logs

  • Estimated dry weight/symptom tracking

  • Dialysis treatment logs

  • Symptoms between treatments

  • Recovery time after dialysis

  • Medication tracker

  • Urine output

  • Nutrition logs

  • Lab results

  • Appointment information

  • Home dialysis treatment logs

  • PD logs

  • Home hemodialysis logs

  • Supply logs

  • Patient questions/concerns submitted to the facility

Treatment Information

Where applicable:

  • Dialysis treatment days

  • Scheduled treatment times

  • Prescribed treatment duration

  • Blood flow rate

  • Dialysate flow rate

  • Dialysate/bath concentration

  • Target/estimated dry weight

  • Access type

  • Home dialysis prescription/order information

Medications

Provider can view:

  • Patient medication list

  • Patient-reported medication adherence

  • Dialysis medications documented by the patient/facility

  • ESA such as Mircera/Epogen

  • IV iron

  • Vitamin D medications

  • Antibiotics

  • Heparin

  • Other dialysis-related medications

Lab Results

Providers can view trends for relevant kidney/dialysis labs, including:

  • Creatinine

  • BUN

  • eGFR

  • Potassium

  • Sodium

  • Calcium

  • Phosphorus

  • Albumin

  • Hemoglobin

  • Hematocrit

  • PTH

  • Ferritin

  • TSAT/iron saturation

  • Bicarbonate/CO2

  • Kt/V

  • URR

  • Glucose/A1C where applicable

Trend graphs would be useful so both the provider and patient can see changes over time.

Communication

Providers should be able to:

  • Receive messages/questions from their assigned patients

  • Respond through the facility/patient messaging system

  • See relevant patient alerts or flagged information

  • See when a patient has exported/shared information with that facility

NephroReach is not intended to replace the organization’s EHR.

2. What information can the Provider edit?

Provider permissions should be more restricted than viewing permissions.

Providers should be able to enter or update:

Provider/Facility-Managed Information

  • Treatment schedule

  • Scheduled treatment time

  • Dialysis prescription/order information

  • Estimated dry weight

  • Access type

  • Medication list when appropriate

  • Dialysis medication information

  • Lab results

  • Upcoming appointments/home visits

  • Patient education status

  • Patient program/enrollment status

Providers should also be able to add a note or comment to certain patient-submitted logs if we choose to activate that feature.

Providers should NOT overwrite patient-entered logs.

For example, if a patient records:

  • BP 165/92

  • Post-dialysis recovery time of 4 hours

  • Shortness of breath

  • Weight gain

the provider should not be able to change what the patient originally documented.

Instead, the system should preserve the original entry.

If corrections are necessary, changes should be recorded with:

  • Who changed it

  • What was changed

  • Date/time

  • Original value

  • New value

This creates an audit trail.

3. Examples of kidney/dialysis lab reports

NephroReach does not need to duplicate the exact visual appearance of laboratory company reports.

We mainly need to capture the important data fields.

Example CKD Lab Result

Basic/Comprehensive Metabolic Panel

TestResultReference Range
Creatinine2.4 mg/dL0.6–1.2
BUN38 mg/dL7–20
eGFR24 mL/min/1.73m²>60
Potassium5.1 mmol/L3.5–5.1
Sodium138 mmol/L136–145
CO2/Bicarbonate20 mmol/L22–29
Calcium8.7 mg/dL8.5–10.5
Albumin3.8 g/dL3.5–5.0

Example Dialysis Monthly Lab Report

TestResult
Hemoglobin10.4 g/dL
Ferritin620 ng/mL
TSAT27%
Potassium4.8 mmol/L
Calcium8.9 mg/dL
Phosphorus5.6 mg/dL
PTH480 pg/mL
Albumin3.7 g/dL
Kt/V1.45
URR72%

The software should store:

  • Lab name

  • Result

  • Unit

  • Reference range if available

  • Abnormal flag if supplied

  • Collection date

  • Result date

  • Source: Patient Entered / Provider Entered / Imported

  • Optional uploaded lab report/document

The patient should be able to see simple trends rather than only a large table of numbers.

4. What systems do Providers currently use for labs?

Different NephroReach customers will use different systems.

Potential customers may use:

  • Their organization’s EHR

  • Dialysis-specific clinical systems

  • Hospital EHRs

  • Independent laboratory portals

  • Internal facility systems

Therefore, NephroReach should NOT be built around one specific provider system.

Phase 1 – Launch

Do NOT require EHR integration.

Allow:

Patient entry
Patient manually enters labs.

Provider entry
Authorized staff manually enters labs.

Document upload
Patient or authorized staff may upload a lab report when appropriate.

Each lab result should clearly display its source.

Example:

Potassium: 4.9 mmol/L
Source: Provider Entered
Collected: September 2, 2026

or

Potassium: 4.9 mmol/L
Source: Patient Entered – Not independently verified

Future Phase

Build API/FHIR integrations for organizations that want automated data transfer.

The system architecture should therefore allow integrations later without requiring them for launch.

5. Will Providers manage lab results directly through NephroReach?

Yes, I want this capability, but it should be OPTIONAL for each organization.

If an organization chooses to use it:

Provider enters:

Patient → Lab Results → Add Result

Then selects:

  • Lab

  • Value

  • Unit

  • Collection date

  • Optional reference range

  • Optional note

Once submitted, the result automatically appears in the patient’s NephroReach account.

The patient’s trend chart should also update automatically.

Providers should also have the option to enter several monthly dialysis labs at once instead of entering each lab individually.

For example:

Monthly Dialysis Labs – September 2026

  • Hemoglobin

  • Albumin

  • Potassium

  • Calcium

  • Phosphorus

  • PTH

  • Ferritin

  • TSAT

  • Kt/V

  • URR

This would be considerably faster for dialysis staff.

Do NOT remove patient self-entry because not every participating facility will enter labs.

6. Legal, privacy and compliance requirements

Because NephroReach may store identifiable patient information and may receive information from nephrology offices, hospitals, and dialysis organizations, the platform should be architected for strong healthcare privacy/security controls.

For organizations subject to HIPAA, HIPAA requires appropriate administrative, physical and technical safeguards for electronic PHI. Technical safeguards include access control, authentication, audit controls, integrity protections and transmission security. (HHS.gov)

If NephroReach creates, receives, maintains or transmits PHI on behalf of a HIPAA-covered healthcare organization, NephroReach may function as that organization’s Business Associate, which ordinarily requires a Business Associate Agreement. Relevant subcontractors that handle PHI may also need appropriate contractual safeguards. (HHS.gov)

Therefore, the developers should build for:

Role-Based Access Control

Different permissions for:

  • NephroReach Admin

  • Organization Admin

  • Provider/Staff

  • Patient

  • Caregiver

Organization/Tenant Isolation

This is extremely important.

Facility A must NEVER see Facility B’s patients.

Every patient/provider record should be associated with an organization/facility ID and access should be enforced on the backend, not only hidden in the user interface.

Patient-Level Access

Provider access should be restricted to patients assigned to that provider/facility.

Authentication

  • Unique user accounts

  • Strong password requirements

  • MFA capability

  • Secure password reset

  • Session expiration

  • Automatic logout where appropriate

Audit Logs

Record important actions such as:

  • Login

  • Failed login

  • Patient record viewed

  • Patient information changed

  • Lab added/edited

  • Provider added/removed

  • Caregiver access granted/revoked

  • File downloaded/exported

  • Message accessed where appropriate

  • Permission changed

Audit logs should include:

  • User

  • Action

  • Patient/account affected

  • Date/time

  • Relevant organization

Encryption

Sensitive data should be protected:

  • In transit

  • At rest

Patient Consent

Patients should explicitly authorize caregiver access.

The system should record:

  • Who was authorized

  • Permission level

  • Date access was granted

  • Date access was revoked

Minimum Access

Users should have access only to the information necessary for their role. HIPAA’s minimum-necessary framework generally calls for limiting PHI access and disclosure to what is reasonably necessary for the intended purpose, although certain treatment disclosures between providers have specific exceptions. (HHS.gov)

Important Development Requirement

Please do not assume that using a “HIPAA-compliant server” alone makes the application compliant.

Security needs to exist throughout:

  • Database

  • Application code

  • Authentication

  • Permissions

  • File storage

  • Backups

  • Messaging

  • Logging

  • APIs

  • Third-party vendors

  • Administrative access

We will obtain healthcare privacy/legal review before production use involving PHI.

7. Caregiver Access

Caregivers should NOT automatically receive full access to a patient’s account.

The patient should control caregiver permissions.

When inviting a caregiver, the patient should enter the caregiver’s email/phone and select what the caregiver is allowed to access.

Recommended Caregiver Permissions

View Health Dashboard

  • Yes/No

View Dialysis Schedule

  • Yes/No

View Treatment Logs

  • Yes/No

View BP/Weight/Fluid Logs

  • Yes/No

View Medications

  • Yes/No

View Medication Reminders

  • Yes/No

View Lab Results

  • Yes/No

View Appointments

  • Yes/No

View Education Content

  • Yes/No

View Patient Journal

  • Default should be NO

The patient’s private reflection/personal journal should remain private unless the patient specifically chooses to share it.

Receive Reminders

  • Yes/No

Examples:

  • Dialysis appointment

  • Medication reminder

  • Home visit

  • Upcoming appointment

Help Manage Medication Tracker

  • Optional permission

Help Manage Appointments

  • Optional permission

Send Messages

  • Optional permission

Caregiver messages should identify the caregiver as the sender rather than appearing to have been written by the patient.

Recommended Caregiver Levels

To make setup easier, we can offer three presets.

View Only

Can see the information the patient chooses but cannot change anything.

Support

Can view selected information and help manage:

  • Appointments

  • Reminders

  • Medication checklist

  • Treatment schedule

Custom

Patient individually selects every permission.

I recommend Custom permissions as the underlying system even if presets are offered in the interface.

Important Backend Relationship

The structure should be:

Organization
→ Providers/Staff
→ Patients assigned to that organization

Patient
→ Patient account
→ Optional Caregiver(s)

A caregiver’s permissions come from the patient, not the provider or organization.

A provider’s permissions come from the organization/facility.

NephroReach Admin should be a separate administrative role and should not use Provider permissions.

Overall Goal

NephroReach should remain a patient engagement, education, communication and tracking platform rather than becoming a replacement electronic health record.

For launch, prioritize:

  1. Role-based permissions

  2. Facility-level patient isolation

  3. Provider dashboard

  4. Patient-generated logs

  5. Provider-entered labs

  6. Lab trends

  7. Secure patient/provider messaging

  8. Caregiver permission controls

  9. Audit logging

  10. Ability to support API/FHIR integrations later

EHR/laboratory integrations can be a later phase rather than delaying launch.

One design decision here is especially important: I would not give caregivers blanket access and I would not let providers silently modify patient-entered data. Both should be permission-based and auditable. That will give your developers a much cleaner architecture and make NephroReach easier to sell to healthcare organizations.

4. Lab Entry & Integration

Different NephroReach customers will use different EHR, dialysis, hospital and laboratory systems. Therefore, NephroReach should NOT depend on one specific external system.

Phase 1 – Launch

NephroReach should support three methods of adding lab results:

Method 1 – Patient Manual Entry

Patients can manually enter their own lab results.

These results should display:

Source: Patient Entered – Not independently verified

Method 2 – Provider Manual Entry

Authorized facility staff can manually enter lab results for an individual patient.

The result should automatically appear in that patient's NephroReach account.

Method 3 – Facility CSV Bulk Lab Upload

This is a required Phase 1 feature.

Authorized facility staff should be able to upload a CSV containing lab results for multiple enrolled patients at once.

Example workflow:

Provider Dashboard → Lab Management → Bulk Upload → Upload CSV

NephroReach should provide a downloadable CSV template.

Recommended CSV fields:

  • NephroReach Patient ID or Facility Patient ID

  • Patient first name

  • Patient last name

  • Date of birth

  • Lab collection date

  • Lab name/test code

  • Lab result/value

  • Unit

  • Reference range low

  • Reference range high

  • Abnormal flag if available

The system should primarily match patients using a unique patient identifier rather than name alone.

Import Validation

Before importing anything, NephroReach should validate the CSV.

The system should display:

Matched Patients: 47
Unmatched Patients: 2
Invalid Lab Results: 1
Ready to Import: 46

The facility should have to review and confirm the import before the results are posted.

The system should NOT automatically guess when it cannot confidently match a patient.

For unmatched patients, staff should be able to review the row and select the correct enrolled patient or exclude the row.

Duplicate Protection

NephroReach should check for potential duplicate lab results using information such as:

  • Patient

  • Lab/test

  • Collection date

  • Result

Potential duplicates should be flagged before import rather than silently creating duplicate results.

After Import

Once confirmed:

CSV → Patient Matching → Validation → Import → Individual Patient Lab Records

The appropriate labs should automatically appear in each patient's account.

For example, one CSV containing monthly dialysis labs for 80 patients could populate the appropriate lab results for all 80 patients instead of staff manually entering each patient's labs.

The patient's existing lab trend graphs should update automatically.

Imported results should display:

Source: Facility CSV Import

CSV Security/Audit Requirements

The system should record:

  • Facility that uploaded the CSV

  • Staff user who uploaded it

  • Date/time uploaded

  • Original filename

  • Number of patient records processed

  • Number successfully imported

  • Number rejected

  • Import errors

  • Import batch ID

Only authorized users from that organization should be able to upload labs.

CSV data must be processed within the same organization/tenant boundaries. A facility's upload must NEVER update or expose patients belonging to another organization.

The developer should also establish a secure policy for temporary CSV files after processing so PHI-containing files are not unnecessarily retained.

Future Phase

Later, NephroReach can support:

EHR/Lab System → API/FHIR Interface → NephroReach

This could automate lab transmission for larger customers.

However, API/FHIR integration is not required for launch.

CSV bulk upload gives organizations a low-cost bridge between their existing systems and NephroReach.

Manual individual entry

CSV bulk upload

  • Encryption in transit

  • Secure file handling

  • Patient consent management

  • Caregiver authorization/revocation

  • Appropriate backups

  • Vendor/subcontractor security controls

Facility A must NEVER see Facility B's patients or data.

This applies to individual records AND bulk CSV uploads.

A CSV uploaded by Facility A must only be capable of matching patients belonging to Facility A.

Security must be enforced by the backend/database, not merely by hiding information in the user interface.

NephroReach will obtain appropriate healthcare privacy/legal review before production use involving PHI.

7. Caregiver Access

Patient Journal

The patient's private reflection/personal journal should remain private unless the patient specifically chooses to share it.

Caregiver Presets

View Only: Can see patient-selected information but cannot modify anything.

Support: Can view selected information and assist with appointments, reminders, medication checklist and treatment schedule.

Custom: Patient chooses individual permissions.

Custom permissions should be the underlying system even if presets are offered for convenience.

Caregiver messages should identify the caregiver as the sender and should never appear as though they were written by the patient.

Patient

Caregiver permissions come from the patient.

Launch Priorities

  2. Facility/tenant isolation

  3. Provider dashboard

  4. Patient-generated logs

  6. Facility CSV bulk lab upload

  7. CSV validation and patient matching

The CSV bulk upload should be considered an important launch feature because it allows facilities to efficiently provide patient lab results without requiring an expensive EHR integration.

That gives you a good middle ground: you don't have to build Epic/Fresenius/DaVita-style integrations at launch, but a facility with 50–100 patients doesn't have to manually enter hundreds of monthly lab values either.

6. HIPAA, PHI Protection & Cybersecurity – LAUNCH-BLOCKING REQUIREMENT

Security is one of the highest priorities for NephroReach.

NephroReach will handle sensitive health information. HIPAA compliance, PHI protection, cybersecurity, privacy and prevention of unauthorized access or data breaches must be incorporated into the architecture from the beginning.

These are NOT post-launch enhancements.

If required security controls have not been implemented and independently tested, the production platform should not launch with real PHI.

No developer or hosting provider can guarantee that a system is "unhackable." The requirement is instead to implement appropriate safeguards, minimize attack surfaces, continuously maintain security, detect unauthorized activity and reduce the probability and impact of a breach.

Required Security Architecture

1. Strict Tenant Isolation

This is critical.

Facility A must NEVER be able to access Facility B's patients, files, messages, labs or other PHI.

Tenant isolation must be enforced at the backend/database/API authorization level—not simply by hiding information in the interface.

Every request for protected data must verify the user's organization and authorization.

2. Role-Based Access Control

Separate permissions must exist for:

  • NephroReach Admin

  • Organization Admin

  • Provider/Staff

  • Patient

  • Caregiver

Users should receive only the minimum access required for their role.

3. Multi-Factor Authentication

MFA should be required for privileged accounts, including:

  • NephroReach administrators

  • Organization administrators

  • Provider/staff accounts

4. Encryption

PHI must be protected using strong, current encryption standards:

In transit: secure HTTPS/TLS.

At rest: databases, backups, file storage and other systems containing PHI should be encrypted.

Encryption keys and secrets must be securely managed and must never be hard-coded into source code or exposed in public repositories.

5. Secure Authentication & Sessions

Implement:

  • Strong authentication

  • Secure password hashing

  • MFA

  • Secure password reset

  • Session expiration

  • Secure cookies/tokens

  • Logout/session revocation

  • Protection against brute-force login attempts

  • Rate limiting

  • Account lockout or equivalent protections where appropriate

6. Comprehensive Audit Logging

NephroReach should maintain security/audit records for important activity, including:

  • Successful login

  • Failed login

  • Patient record accessed

  • PHI viewed where appropriate

  • PHI changed

  • Lab upload

  • CSV import

  • File upload/download

  • Provider added/removed

  • Permission changes

  • Caregiver authorization/revocation

  • Exports

  • Administrative actions

Logs should identify:

  • User

  • Organization

  • Action

  • Date/time

  • Relevant patient/resource

  • Appropriate security metadata

Audit logs themselves must be protected from unauthorized alteration.

7. Secure File Uploads

All uploaded files—including lab reports, access photographs and CSV files—must be treated as potentially unsafe.

Implement controls such as:

  • File type validation

  • File size restrictions

  • Malware scanning

  • Secure/private storage

  • Randomized storage identifiers

  • Authorization checks before every file retrieval

  • No publicly accessible PHI URLs

  • Appropriate deletion/retention policies

8. API Security

Every API endpoint involving protected information must perform authorization checks.

Never rely solely on the frontend to determine whether someone is allowed to see data.

The system should protect against common web application attacks, including:

  • Broken access control

  • Injection attacks

  • Cross-site scripting

  • Cross-site request forgery where applicable

  • Credential attacks

  • ID/URL manipulation

  • Unauthorized API requests

  • Excessive request/abuse attacks

9. Database Security

Production databases containing PHI should:

  • Not be publicly accessible

  • Have restricted network access

  • Use least-privilege credentials

  • Be encrypted

  • Be securely backed up

  • Have access logged/monitored

  • Use separate production credentials

  • Never expose production PHI in development/test environments

Developers should use synthetic/test patient information during development and QA whenever possible.

10. Secure Development Process

Security testing must occur BEFORE launch.

This should include:

  • Code review

  • Dependency/vulnerability scanning

  • Authentication testing

  • Authorization testing

  • Tenant-isolation testing

  • API security testing

  • File-upload security testing

  • Database/security configuration review

  • Secrets scanning

  • Backup/restore testing

11. Independent Penetration Testing

Before NephroReach begins storing real PHI, an independent qualified cybersecurity professional/company should perform penetration and vulnerability testing.

The person who built the application should not be the only person validating its security.

Critical and high-risk findings should be corrected and retested before production launch.

12. Monitoring & Incident Detection

Production infrastructure should support:

  • Security monitoring

  • Failed-login monitoring

  • Suspicious activity detection

  • Application/server monitoring

  • Security alerts

  • Vulnerability/dependency monitoring

  • Incident investigation

13. Backups & Disaster Recovery

Encrypted backups should be maintained and tested.

NephroReach should have documented procedures for:

  • Data restoration

  • Service outages

  • Security incidents

  • Disaster recovery

Backups should receive the same security protections as production PHI.

14. Third-Party Vendors

Any third party that creates, receives, maintains or transmits PHI for NephroReach must be evaluated before use.

Where required, appropriate Business Associate Agreements must be in place.

This includes evaluating services used for:

  • Hosting

  • Databases

  • File storage

  • Backups

  • Email/SMS involving PHI

  • Analytics

  • Error logging

  • Customer support

  • AI services

  • APIs

  • Other subprocessors

PHI must not be sent to a third-party service simply because that service is convenient.

15. Production vs Development

Production PHI must be isolated from:

  • Development

  • Staging

  • Demo environments

  • Developer laptops

  • Personal accounts

Developers should not download real patient databases or PHI onto personal devices.

16. HIPAA Security Risk Analysis

Before launch with real PHI, NephroReach should complete and document a HIPAA security risk analysis and address identified vulnerabilities and risks.

Security and HIPAA compliance are ongoing operational responsibilities—not a one-time development checklist.

7. Caregiver Access

Caregivers should NOT automatically receive full access.

Patients should control caregiver permissions.

Available permissions can include:

  • Health dashboard

  • Dialysis schedule

  • Treatment logs

  • BP/weight/fluid information

  • Medications

  • Medication reminders

  • Lab results

  • Appointments

  • Education

  • Selected reminders

  • Medication tracker assistance

  • Appointment management

  • Messaging

The patient's private journal should default to NO caregiver access unless the patient specifically shares it.

Caregiver activity must occur through the caregiver's own authenticated account so activity can be attributed to the correct individual.

NEPHROREACH LAUNCH PRIORITIES

These requirements are not ranked solely by feature importance. Security surrounds every feature.

  1. HIPAA security/privacy architecture and PHI protection

  2. Strict organization/tenant data isolation

  3. Role-based access control and least-privilege permissions

  4. Encryption in transit and at rest

  5. Strong authentication and MFA for privileged users

  6. Comprehensive audit logging

  7. Secure database, file storage, backups and infrastructure

  8. Secure application/API development

  9. Security monitoring and incident-response capability

  10. Independent vulnerability assessment/penetration testing before real PHI

  11. Provider dashboard and facility-specific patient access

  12. Patient-generated logs

  13. Provider-entered labs

  14. Facility CSV bulk lab upload

  15. CSV validation and secure processing

  16. Lab trends

  17. Secure patient/provider messaging

  18. Caregiver permission controls

  19. Backup/disaster recovery testing

  20. Architecture capable of supporting future API/FHIR integrations

Launch Gate

NephroReach should NOT go live with real patient PHI simply because the functional features are complete.

Production launch with PHI should occur only after the required privacy/security controls are implemented, security testing is completed, significant vulnerabilities are remediated and the appropriate HIPAA/privacy/compliance requirements for NephroReach's operating model have been addressed.

That wording gives your developers a much stronger requirement than saying “make it HIPAA compliant.” It also makes tenant isolation especially critical: one of the scenarios your independent QA/security tester should specifically try to exploit is whether a provider at Clinic A can manipulate an ID, URL, API request, CSV, or account permission to access even one patient at Clinic B. That should be treated as a launch-blocking failure.
